HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bedroom Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bedroom as a sequence in disguise: the five words are the five moves of bedtime, and the child learns them by doing them.

What is this?

The bedroom keeps the bed, the pillow, the blanket, the wardrobe (the closet) and the bedside table — the five things between waking and sleeping.

What does it mean?

Bedtime resists being told and accepts being known. When the child can name and run the sequence — pillow, blanket, book, light — bedtime stops being something that happens to them.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the actual bedtime, which is the perfect classroom: the lesson IS the routine tonight, with each word said as each thing happens.

Why this matters

The wardrobe-closet pair rides along free: whichever your family says, the child now owns both names for the same door. Bedside table is the bonus word — it belongs to the child.

What it teaches

Sequencing (first pillow, then blanket, then light), ownership of a routine, and the possessive pride of my bed, my pillow, my table.

Words to learn

bedpillowblanketwardrobeclosetbedside table

Say this to your child

“"Bedroom words, in order: clothes in the wardrobe, pillow up, blanket down, book on the bedside table, light off. You know the whole goodnight by heart."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card at the bedroom door: "five words, and we will do every one of them tonight."
  2. Wardrobe first: open it, name the clothes hanging there — closet or wardrobe, say yours, offer both.
  3. Bed next: pillow fluffed by small hands, blanket spread by the same.
  4. Book on the bedside table — the table gets its word as the book lands.
  5. Light off with the fifth word: "bedroom words — all five. Goodnight."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Bedroom Words" sit over a made bed, a soft pillow, a folded blanket with a stripe, a tall wardrobe with two doors and a small bedside table with a drawer.

Ask your child

"Where do the clothes sleep?" (the wardrobe — the closet) "What holds your head?" "Where does the storybook live until morning?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might recite the five in bed like a countdown, insist the teddy has its own bedside spot, or teach the sequence to the wardrobe itself.

Out in the real world

Every bed away from home — hotel, grandma’s, holiday — still has a pillow, a blanket and a light. The sequence goes where the child goes, and strange bedrooms shrink to familiar words.

Try it together

Goodnight Countdown: the five words written (or drawn) on a card by the bed; the child taps each one as it happens tonight. Five taps and the card says goodnight first.

Understanding check

Ask: "What goes on first, the pillow or the blanket?" (pillow) "Where do we keep clothes?" (the wardrobe or closet) "What is the little table by the bed?" (the bedside table)

This lesson pairs with the Bedroom Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.
